A.explanation: Force from atmosphere is $(\text{atmospheric pressure}) \times A$ and it acts through distance $r$, so work is $(\text{atmospheric pressure}) \times Ar$.

B.explanation: Length $s$ is the final total length of the gas column, not the distance moved, so $As$ is the final volume not the change in volume.

C.explanation: This is the total work done by the expanding gas, but part of it works against friction since the piston is not frictionless.

D.explanation: It uses the wrong pressure and the wrong length, as $As$ is the final volume and gas pressure includes work against friction.

hints: Look at the diagram: the piston moves from P to Q through distance $r$, while $s$ is the whole length of the gas column after expansion.
Work done against the atmosphere must use atmospheric pressure, not pressure inside the gas, because the piston is not frictionless and gas pressure also overcomes friction.
Combine force on the piston from the atmosphere, $(\text{atmospheric pressure}) \times A$, with work $= $ force $\times$ distance moved.
walkthrough: Identify the motion: area is $A$ and the piston is pushed back a distance $r$ from P to Q, so the increase in gas volume is $\Delta V = Ar$.
State the rule for work against a constant pressure: $W = Fd$ with $F = pA$, so $W = pA \times d = p\Delta V$.
For work against the atmosphere only, use $p = $ atmospheric pressure and $d = r$, giving $W = (\text{atmospheric pressure}) \times A \times r$.
Check the distractors: $s$ gives the final volume $As$, not the change $Ar$, and pressure inside the gas gives total work by the gas including work against friction.
Therefore the work done against the atmosphere alone is $(\text{atmospheric pressure}) \times Ar$. This is option A.
